title: Together AI says its own coding agent committed the credential that leaked customer prompts
subtitle: The disclosed incident fits a growing pattern: autonomous coding agents pushing secrets into public repositories faster than the humans reviewing them can catch.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Together AI disclosed on November 21, 2026 that an AI coding agent working on its public `xorl` GitHub repository committed a credential granting access to a private Hugging Face repository holding stored prompt samples. Before the company's automated scanning caught the credential and reverted the commit, an unauthorized party downloaded serverless prompt samples from June and July 2026. Affected models named in the coverage include MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6. Together says it believes the downloaded data has since been deleted, has engaged an external forensic firm and law enforcement, and has made zero data retention the default for new accounts. The exposure window and the number of affected prompts remain undisclosed.

The twist in this incident is the identity of the attacker-of-opportunity: Together's own coding agent. The agent, not a human engineer, pushed the credential. That inverts how security teams usually model repo hygiene — the assumption that credentials leak when a tired human copies a file is still true, but the incident rate is now dominated by agents that can push 20 times faster than any human reviewer. Together's response — scoped or short-lived credentials, credential checks on pull requests, and new rules for AI coding agents — is the right shape, but it is also a retrofit onto a workflow that never had an agent in the threat model.

This slots into a stack of 2026 agent-driven credential incidents: the Cursor/Fireworks AI key theft via a backdoored Claude Code extension that hit roughly 5,000 developers (November 16), the LiteLLM supply chain breach touching 2,500 organizations (August 13), Hugging Face's own autonomous-agent breach disclosure (July 18), and the OpenRouter off-boarding this weekend of three inference providers from Zero Data Retention eligibility. The through-line is that agent-driven development has outrun the git hooks, CI scanners, and code-review norms that assume a human is at the keyboard.

A note for learners: the mitigation that scales is not 'make the agent smarter about secrets' — it is 'remove the blast radius before the agent can touch it.' Short-lived credentials that expire in minutes, broker services that mediate access, and OIDC-based access that never requires a long-lived token in a repo at all. If you are building anything that lets a model commit to a repository, assume the model will commit a credential within the first thousand pull requests. Then design for the moment after that, not before it.
